text: AAFCO Large Breed Dog Growth: the 2026 AAFCO Growth and Reproduction profile for dogs with its lower calcium max, 4.5 g/Mcal (1.8% DM) instead of 6.25 g/Mcal (2.5% DM). The 2026 AAFCO applies this max to formulas that may be fed to large size puppies, those weighing 70 lb (about 31.8 kg) or more as mature lean adults (Footnote d, page 167; Footnote e, page 165), and, unless a product's labeling restricts it to specific breeds, to products bearing an All Life Stages claim based on being formulated to the Growth and Reproduction profile (page 170); for other life stages, including non-large-breed growth formulas, the calcium max is 6.25 g/Mcal (2.5% DM), as under AAFCO Dog Growth (Small & Medium) and Reproduction. Large size dog growth products and all life stages products substantiated by AAFCO feeding protocols using non-large size dogs must also contain no more than the large size calcium and phosphorus maxs (pages 162 and 186). In this sheet the two AAFCO dog growth selections differ only in this calcium max and in the energy min (this one covers growth only; see the AA4 note). The expected mature BW in E3 on the Standards sheet is not used by the AAFCO selections, so choose this selection for a puppy expected to weigh 70 lb (about 31.8 kg) or more as a lean adult, and for an All Life Stages dog food not restricted to specific breeds (see the O1 note on the Standards sheet).

text: Where 0.000000001 is added to a maximum in this column, it represents a 2006 NRC adult dog maintenance safe upper limit (SUL) given as a greater-than value; the amount added is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision. The same rule is used in columns F, N, V, X and AH. Used for sodium only: F60 = 15/4+0.000000001 (3.750000001 g/Mcal, from >15 g/kg DM in 2006 NRC Table 15-5). F61 = 0.4913 (the sodium MBW max derived from >15 g/kg DM; see the F61 note) carries no addition, as it is this sheet's own estimate, not a limit NRC prints. Iodine (F76, F77) has no addition, as NRC prints that SUL as >=4 mg/kg DM, not >4. A value equal to the limit itself is described as Highest (90% of Range or Greater) on the Standards sheet with or without the addition. Because the Standards sheet compares values at 7 decimal places, the addition does not change how any entered value is described. The MBW maximums in this column (F37, F39, F45, F61, F63, F77, F83, F85 and F87; F61, F63 and F77 are this sheet's estimates, see their notes) are kept as printed in 2006 NRC Table 15-5 per kg BW^0.75. The Standards sheet converts them with the energy in C11, so they equal the per Mcal SULs within about 4% only at 130 * BW^0.75 (the average laboratory or active dog type): e.g., the fat MBW max (10.8 g/kg BW^0.75) converts to about 83.1 g/Mcal at 130, but to 54 g/Mcal for the Great Dane type (200 * BW^0.75) and about 113.7 g/Mcal for the inactive type (95 * BW^0.75), against the 82.5 g/Mcal fat SUL in F36, and an intake entered in K4 moves it the same way. So for very active types a diet within the per Mcal SUL can read above the MBW row's max; per day, a dog eating 200 kcal/kg BW^0.75 at 82.5 g fat/Mcal takes in 16.5 g fat/kg BW^0.75, above NRC's 10.8. Table 15-5 Footnote b (page 360) asks for the per kg BW^0.75 amounts for dogs with an unusually low energy intake.

text: For FEDIAF Dog (MER 95 kcal/kg^0.75) and FEDIAF Dog (MER 110 kcal/kg^0.75): the MBW rows in these columns hold the FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Table VII-11 (page 58) minimums per kg BW^0.75 for adult dog maintenance, as printed; FEDIAF gives one adult dog column for both MERs. Units are converted where this sheet's unit differs (chloride 0.04 g = 40 mg, magnesium 0.02 g = 20 mg, cobalamin 0.92 mcg = 0.00092 mg); folic acid is divided by 0.6 to mcg DFE (=7.1/0.6), as on the folate row; and retinol is the vitamin A IU * 0.3, as on the retinol row. The Standards sheet converts them to per Mcal with the energy in C11: with no intake entered in K4 they give about this column's per Mcal values (e.g., protein 4.95 * 1,000/110 = 45 g/Mcal under MER 110), and with an intake entered in K4 they give the concentration FEDIAF calls for at that intake (FEDIAF section 7.2.5, pages 59-60: units/1,000 kcal = nutrient requirement per day per kg metabolic BW * 1,000 / energy intake per kg metabolic BW). Table VII-11 is rounded to 2 decimal places, so some converted values differ from the per Mcal values (e.g., sodium 0.03 * 1,000/95 = 0.3158 g/Mcal versus 0.29 g/Mcal; figures rounded; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision). The Standards sheet checks each MBW row and its per Mcal row separately, so a diet meets both only when it meets the higher one. Table VII-11 gives minimums only. For the 13 MBW rows whose per Mcal row has a max (calcium, phosphorus, sodium, chloride, iron, copper, manganese, zinc, iodine, selenium, retinol, vitamin A and vitamin D), the MBW row's max in the MAX column is this application's own calculation, not a FEDIAF value: the per Mcal max * the MER / 1,000, the relation of FEDIAF section 7.2.5 applied to a max (e.g., vitamin D 800 * 95/1,000 = 76 IU/kg BW^0.75 under MER 95). With no intake entered in K4 it converts back to the per Mcal max, so both rows' ranges end at the same max; with an intake entered in K4 it converts to another concentration, as the min does, while the per Mcal row keeps FEDIAF's max at any intake. Its type is CALC (see the AU3 note): a value above it is described as Highest (90% of Range or Greater), and the Open Animal Nutrition FHIR IG does not call it excess. The other MBW rows have no max (range high 4 times the min). Fat MBW reads none: FEDIAF states that the fat minimum for a MER of 95 kcal/kg BW^0.75 has not been adjusted for energy intake (page 23), and Table VII-11's 1.51 g/kg BW^0.75 fits the MER 110 value only (13.75 * 0.110 = 1.5125). The Selenium, Se MBW row uses the dry diet value (5.20 mcg/kg BW^0.75) for every food; Table VII-11's wet diet value (6.40) is not used, as the Standards sheet has no Selenium, Se (For >12% Moisture Foods) MBW row (see its B91 note). So with an intake entered in K4 below the MER, a food of more than 12% moisture can be asked for up to about 19% less selenium than FEDIAF's wet diet value gives at that intake (5.20 versus 6.40): e.g., under MER 110 at 80 kcal/kg BW^0.75, FEDIAF's equation gives 80 mcg/Mcal for a wet diet (6.40 * 1,000/80), while this sheet asks 65 on the MBW row (5.20 * 1,000/80) and 57.5 on the >12% moisture per Mcal row. Up to version 18OCT26 these MBW cells read none.

text: Maximums in this column (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Tables III-3a and III-3b, pages 15 and 16): FEDIAF gives nutritional maximums (N) and EU legal maximums (L). This application uses the nutritional maximum wherever FEDIAF gives one, and the legal maximum only where it gives none; the sodium and chloride maximums are FEDIAF's Footnote c safe levels (see their notes). A legal maximum applies only when that trace element or vitamin is added to the recipe as an additive, and then to the total amount in the food; when it comes only from feed materials, the legal maximum does not apply, and only a nutritional maximum, where FEDIAF gives one, does (section 3.1.3, page 11). FEDIAF gives no nutritional maximum for copper, iodine, iron, manganese, selenium or zinc, so for these the legal maximum is used here for every diet, supplemented or not, as this application's cautious choice. FEDIAF gives the legal maximums per kg dry matter (DM) only, as they do not account for energy density (page 13); per 100 g DM: copper 2.80 mg, iodine 1.10 mg, iron 68.18 mg, manganese 17.00 mg, selenium 56.80 mcg and zinc 22.70 mg. This column converts them at 4 kcal ME/g DM (e.g., iron (681.8/(4*1000))*1000 = 170.45 mg/Mcal), so each equals the legal maximum only for a food of 4 kcal ME/g DM: for a food of 5 kcal ME/g DM the iron legal maximum is 136.36 mg/Mcal, and for a food of 3.5 kcal ME/g DM it is 194.8 mg/Mcal. To check a food against a legal maximum, compare its amount per kg DM. For vitamin D, FEDIAF gives both: this column uses the nutritional maximum, 800 IU/1,000 kcal ME (320 IU/100 g DM), which FEDIAF sets for growing giant breed dogs and recommends for the other life stages (page 26; it considers 425 IU/100 g DM safe for small breed puppies); when vitamin D is added as an additive, the EU legal maximum of 227 IU/100 g DM (567.5 IU/Mcal at 4 kcal ME/g DM) applies as well. The MBW rows' maximums in this column are not FEDIAF values: each is the per Mcal max in the row above * the MER / 1,000, calculated by this application (type CALC; see the I3 note).

This sheet keeps the MBW values for both cat types: with the overweight equation (130 * BWkg^0.4), the MBW rows convert to about 1.12 to 1.35 times the per Mcal values for cats of 4 to 8 kg (0.769 * BWkg^0.27; figures rounded; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision), so for an overweight cat they ask more than the per Mcal rows. text: From 2006 NRC, Table 15-5 Footnote i 1 microgram cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) = 40 IU vitamin D3. Morris of UC Davis in 2002 showed that cats used vitamin D2 with an efficiency of 70% as compared to vitamin D3 (J Anim Physiol Anim Nutr (Berl). 2002; 86(7-8):229-38.). The 2006 NRC (page 201) states that in most species vitamin D3 is used with equal or greater efficiency than vitamin D2, citing cats, and does not state this for dogs; but it has been known since 1939 that dogs utilize vitamin D2 and D3 equally well (Arnold and Elvehjem, J Am Vet Med Assoc. 1939; 95:187-194.). In that first definitive study at the University of Wisconsin, growing dogs grew normally, with radiographic (x-ray) monitoring of bone development (if developmental abnormalities appeared) and blood calcium and phosphorus levels, over a five month experimental period. Later in 1943, Morgan and Shimotori of UC Berkeley showed that the same single massive IU dose of either vitamin D2 or vitamin D3 maintained blood calcium levels and vitamin D levels equivalently in growing dogs over the 180 day study (J Biol Chem. 1943; 147:189-200.). It is worth noting that in this study, it appeared that the vitamin D2 may have had a better lasting effect in the last couple of weeks compared to the vitamin D3 sources. text: NRC, AAFCO, and FEDIAF report "folic acid" requirements and not folate; 1 mcg DFE (dietary folate equivalent) = 1 mcg food folate per the US NIH (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Folate-HealthProfessional/ accessed 23SEP25); folate is the vitamin B9 water-soluble vitamin naturally present in foods. Per the NIH: "Folic acid is the fully oxidized monoglutamate form of the vitamin that is used in fortified foods and most dietary supplements." To convert to the common mcg DFE unit that covers all food and fortified/supplemental forms, one divides the Folic Acid value in mcg by 0.6 as 1 mcg DFE = 0.6 mcg folic acid when consumed with food. Every folic acid minimum on this sheet (2006 NRC, 2026 AAFCO and FEDIAF Sept. 2025) is converted this way, so each minimum here is the printed folic acid value expressed in mcg DFE: a diet whose folate comes from added folic acid meets it at the printed amount (e.g., the 2026 AAFCO cat minimum of 0.20 mg folic acid/1,000 kcal ME, page 177, is 333.3 mcg DFE/Mcal), while folate naturally present in foods counts one to one, so a diet relying on food folate needs 1.67 times the printed amount. The 2006 NRC states that its vitamin minimums are the bioavailable forms in the diet at the point of consumption, generally adequate when most of a vitamin comes from a vitamin premix, and that when a vitamin comes mainly from food ingredients the minimum should be modified by a suitable factor (Note on Bioavailability, page 356); FEDIAF Sept. 2025 bases its B vitamin minimums on bioavailable forms from a vitamin premix (pages 27 and 31). The 2026 AAFCO profiles give folic acid with no form or bioavailability basis (pages 166 and 177); AAFCO set its dog value equal to the 2006 NRC adequate intake (page 173) and kept its cat value at or above the 2006 NRC recommended allowance (page 179). The 0.6 comes from human nutrition (the NIH, above), and none of these standards gives a folate factor for dogs or cats, so dividing every folic acid minimum by 0.6 is this sheet's choice, the cautious one when folate comes from food. On the Standards sheet, enter folate as mcg DFE per Mcal: mcg food folate + (mcg folic acid / 0.6).

text: What the values in this table are, and what a band does and does not show. The mins and maxs are the selected requirement's values, in the units of column D (per Mcal on most rows; see the D5 note), or this application's own where its notes say so; they are not all minimum requirements. The 2006 NRC selections use recommended allowances (RA; except where a row's notes say otherwise), which NRC defines as the concentration or amount of a nutrient in a diet formulated to support a given physiological state; the RA is based on the minimal requirement (MR) and, where applicable, includes a safety factor for nutrients with uncertain bioavailability, and where no MR is available, the RA is based on the adequate intake (AI) (2006 NRC page 354). The 2026 AAFCO profiles were designed to establish practical minimum and some maximum nutrient concentrations for dog and cat foods formulated from commonly used, non-purified, complex ingredients, and these concentrations differ from minimum nutrient requirements (2026 AAFCO page 161). The FEDIAF Sept. 2025 values are minimum recommended nutrient levels for commercial pet food, not minimum requirements or optimal intake levels (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 page 14). So a value below a min is below that standard's recommendation, which is not by itself proof that the diet is inadequate for the animal, and a value at or above every min is not by itself proof of adequacy: the 2026 AAFCO (page 162) states that no list of concentrations can invariably ensure that all nutrient requirements are fulfilled in all diet formulas without additional considerations, and that formulating to a profile should not discourage feeding trials. Products substantiated by AAFCO feeding protocols are not mandated to meet the profile mins or maxs, except that large size dog growth and all life stages products substantiated with non-large size dogs must not exceed the large size calcium and phosphorus maxs (2026 AAFCO page 162), and FEDIAF states that pet foods can be adequate and safe with nutrient levels outside its recommendations, based on the manufacturer's substantiation of nutritional adequacy and safety (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 page 10). Some mins are conditional in the standards (e.g., for cats, the 2026 AAFCO states that vitamin K does not need to be added unless the diet contains more than 25% fish on a DM basis, and biotin unless the diet contains antimicrobial or antivitamin compounds; pages 175 and 177); this application applies such mins to every diet (see the B102 and B116 notes). A min or max of "none" means this application uses no value from the selected requirement for that row: usually the requirement gives none (in the 2006 NRC tables the absence of data marks a gap in knowledge, page 354, and the 2026 AAFCO marks some values ND, not determined, e.g., Footnote c, page 167), and in a few columns this application does not use a printed value (see the notes in row 3 of the Healthy Dog Cat Reqt Data sheet). With no max, the range high is derived from the min (see the K1 note); for the kinds of max, see the E5 note. The descriptors only compare the entered values with these ranges; they do not check a nutrient's source or form, digestibility, processing losses or what the entered values represent (see the G1 note).

text: See tan cells' notes on this sheet and the Healthy Dog Cat Reqt Data sheet for details regarding maximums or maxs and if applicable their calculation. The type of each max on the Healthy Dog Cat Reqt Data sheet (e.g., a 2006 NRC SUL, a 2026 AAFCO max, a FEDIAF nutritional or legal max, or this application's own estimate) is recorded beside it in that sheet's columns AU to BO; see the AU3 note there for the codes. Tan marks a noted cell in the table that would otherwise be white; header cells and cells with another colour (e.g., the gray formula cells or the light blue entry cells and their labels) keep their colour when they have a note (hover over a cell to read its note). The kinds of max differ. A 2006 NRC safe upper limit (SUL) is based on the maximal concentration or amount of a nutrient that has not been associated with adverse effects in dogs and cats (2006 NRC page 354); NRC prints some SULs as lower bounds (">" values) and some per kg metabolic body weight (codes SUL>, SULm and SULm>; SULm* where NRC states a per kg SUL only for its reference kitten or queen and this sheet uses it for every one), and its choline max for dogs is a presumed safe maximum given in its text (page 233; code PSM; see the F108 note on the Healthy Dog Cat Reqt Data sheet). The 2026 AAFCO set maxs for nutrients where the potential for overuse or toxicity is of concern; foods that reference its profiles must contain no more than any max listed, and AAFCO states that establishing a maximum concentration implies safety below that concentration for long term consumption (2026 AAFCO pages 162 and 163; code AAFCO). A FEDIAF nutritional maximum (N) is the maximum level of a nutrient in a complete pet food that, based on scientific data, has not been associated with adverse effects in healthy dogs and cats; levels above it may still be safe, but no scientific data are currently known to FEDIAF (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 pages 8 and 11). A FEDIAF legal maximum (L) is an EU limit for nutrients added as additives: it applies only when the nutrient is added to the recipe as an additive, and then to the total amount in the food, and FEDIAF gives it on a dry matter basis only (page 11). A FEDIAF footnote safe level (FSL: sodium under the FEDIAF selections, and chloride under the FEDIAF dog selections) is a level that a FEDIAF table footnote states to be safe, without marking it (N) or (L) (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 page 21; see the B72 note and the AU3 note on the Healthy Dog Cat Reqt Data sheet). Other range highs are this application's: its own estimates or calculations (codes EST, CALC and TPL; see the cell's or row's notes), or, when there is no max, the min times the multiplier in column K (code K; see the K1 note). On a row with a min, whatever the kind of max, a value above the range high is described here as Highest (90% of Range or Greater), as is a value from 90% of the range up to it; on a row with a max but no min, only a value entered under Max (column I) is described by the bands, and a value entered under Min (column G) reads "No min requirement &/or no min amount entered to describe" (on the water row it is not described) (see the L5 note). For the Open Animal Nutrition FHIR IG these kinds are grouped as follows (proposed, pending ratification): authoritative (SUL, SUL>, SULm, SULm>, PSM, AAFCO and N), the only kind above which the IG calls a value excess; conditional (L, FSL, N* and SULm*, the last two being a FEDIAF or NRC max used beyond the life stage or reference animal it is stated for, and AAFCO while the AAFCO dry matter factor in AS3 is above 1, as AAFCO compares a food below 4 kcal/g DM with its dry matter values while the maxs here stay per Mcal; see the C130 note); template-set (EST, CALC and TPL); and derived-provisional (K).

text: Descriptors compare each entered value with the min, max and band edges, both rounded to 7 decimal places (the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision). Each band runs from its lower edge up to, but not including, the next band's lower edge, so a value equal to a band's lower edge belongs to that band; the first band also takes any value below 0 (e.g., a negative carbohydrate by difference), and the top band takes every value at or above its lower edge. On a row where the selected requirement gives no range (no max, and no min or no range above the min), a value that would otherwise be described by a band is described as "No range" instead, unless it is below a stated min. Displayed values are rounded: band edges (columns O to AP) show two decimals, and mins and maxs show their cell's number format. An entered value that looks equal to a displayed min or edge can therefore fall on either side of it; e.g., a min of 25.2307692 displays as 25.23, so an entered 25.23 is below the min and is described as Slightly Restricted. Each band's displayed upper edge (columns P, R, T and so on to AN) is set just below the next band's lower edge (e.g., 0.249999999 instead of 0.25 times the min), so two adjacent edges can display the same number.

text: No automatic adjustment is made to vitamin E concentrations for high PUFA diets which the 2006 NRC recommends increasing in high PUFA diets. See p. 208 for Table 8-2 and the Muggli 1994 proposed formula to calculate if of interest and/or sources of PUFAs requiring high amounts of additional vitamin E are not already fortified like fish oils rich in EPA and DHA. Also see the possible impact of increased vitamin E on vitamin K in Delaney and Dzanis 2018 DOI: 10.2460/javma.252.5.537 . The 2026 AAFCO indicates for dogs (pages 165 and 167), "A diet containing 50 IU of vitamin E will have a ratio >=0.6:1 when the PUFA content is 83 grams or less. Diets containing more than 83 grams of PUFA should contain an additional 0.6 IU of vitamin E for every gram of PUFA." and for cats (pages 175 and 177), "Add 10 IU vitamin E above the minimum concentration for each gram of fish oil per kilogram of diet." AAFCO's dog figures of 50 IU and 83 grams are amounts per kg of dry matter: 50 IU/kg DM is its dog vitamin E minimum in the dry matter table (page 164), given as 12.5 IU per 1,000 kcal ME in its other table (page 166) at its presumed 4,000 kcal ME/kg DM, so 83 grams of PUFA per kg DM is about 20.8 g per 1,000 kcal ME. The 2006 NRC tables give vitamin E in mg alpha-tocopherol, with the footnote 1 IU = 1 mg all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate (footnotes to Tables 15-3, 15-5, 15-8, 15-10, 15-12 and 15-14, pages 358, 360, 363, 365, 367 and 369, referring to its Chapter 8), and this sheet uses the NRC mg as IU one to one (this sheet's choice, following that footnote); for dogs this fits the 2006 NRC adequate intake of 24 IU per 4,000 kcal (page 209), the 6.0 mg per 1,000 kcal of Tables 15-3, 15-5 and 15-8 (pages 358, 360 and 363). In IU per mg, relative to all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate (1.00), the 2006 NRC (page 207) gives all-rac-alpha-tocopherol 1.10, RRR-alpha-tocopheryl acetate 1.36, RRR-alpha-tocopherol (the naturally occurring form) 1.49, all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl succinate 0.89 and RRR-alpha-tocopheryl succinate 1.21 (United States Pharmacopeia 1985, largely from studies in rats; not measured in dogs or cats); FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Table VII-14 (page 63) gives the same factors for the alcohol and acetate forms. The 2006 NRC states that there is no information on vitamin E toxicity in dogs, that Hall et al. (2003) gave dogs 447 mg all-rac-tocopheryl acetate for 17 weeks with no adverse effects (no basis, such as per kg diet, is printed for this amount) and that the NRC (1987) suggested a maximum tolerable level of 1,000 to 2,000 IU/kg diet (page 209). The 2026 AAFCO records that the dog vitamin E maximum was deleted from its profiles because the 2006 NRC had set no safe upper limit, having no information on vitamin E toxicity in dogs (page 173). text: Set at 3.5 kcal/g dry matter (DM) based on the lowest historical threshold in some regulatory guidelines (pre-2016 AAFCO Official Publications (dog profiles)) to switch to using requirements on a dry matter basis instead of an energy basis when a food's energy density is below this value. It is this application's own minimum, not an energy density requirement of the 2006 NRC, 2026 AAFCO, or FEDIAF Sept. 2025, and neither is this row's fixed 6 kcal/g DM range high (see the note in column K of this row). The 2026 AAFCO dog and cat profiles presume 4000 kcal ME/kg DM (4 kcal/g DM) and state that "formulations less than 4000 kcal ME/kg should not be corrected for energy" (Footnote a on pages 164 and 175; page 183 states the same rule), so AAFCO compares such foods, whatever their moisture, with its dry matter values without energy correction. This application compares every food per Mcal, which matches the 2006 NRC (page 355) and FEDIAF Sept. 2025 (page 13), as both correct for any energy density. To apply AAFCO's rule under an AAFCO requirement, when the energy density entered in G130 (this row's Min entry) is above 0 and below 4 kcal/g DM, each min in column C that a caloric restriction entered in G10 raises, and the fat min, is multiplied by 4 divided by that energy density (the AAFCO dry matter factor in AS3; see its note), together with any caloric restriction factor. This equals AAFCO's dry matter comparison to within the rounding between its dry matter and per 1,000 kcal tables: e.g., at 3.6 kcal/g DM the 65 g/Mcal adult cat protein min becomes 72.2 g/Mcal, which is 26% protein in DM. The exception is 7 values that AAFCO prints differently in its two tables (for cats, valine for growth and reproduction, and linoleic acid; for dogs, EPA + DHA, sodium, chloride and selenium for growth and reproduction, and selenium for adult maintenance): for these the factored min corresponds to a dry matter value other than the one AAFCO prints, so a food can meet it here and not AAFCO's dry matter value, or the reverse (see the notes in AI30, O38, AI38, Y44, AA44, Y60, AA60, Y62, AA62, G78, G80, Y78, Y80, AA78 and AA80 on the Healthy Dog Cat Reqt Data sheet). The maximums stay per Mcal, this application's cautious choice, as an animal eating a less energy-dense food to its energy needs takes in the per Mcal amount; so such a food at an AAFCO dry matter maximum can read above the per Mcal maximum here. Nothing is adjusted when G130 is blank or 4 or more, or under an NRC or FEDIAF requirement. AAFCO adds that formulations of low energy density should not be considered adequate for reproductive needs (dogs) or for growth or reproductive needs (cats) based on comparison to the profiles alone (Footnote a on pages 164 and 175). For reference, the 2026 AAFCO (page 167) states that before the 2016 revisions to its profiles the presumed caloric density for dog foods was 3500 kcal ME/kg DM for nutrient concentrations per kg DM.
